hero.name: Bhavesh
hero.who: a 27-year-old medical representative in Ahmedabad whose salary vanishes before month end

story.b: On the first of every month, Bhavesh's phone buzzes with his salary message, and for one day he feels rich. He spends his weeks riding his bike across Ahmedabad, visiting clinics with a bag full of medicine samples, and he works hard. Yet by the twentieth he is borrowing from his roommate Hardik for petrol. There is an EMI on his new phone and another on the bike he upgraded last Diwali. Most nights he orders dinner because he is too tired to cook. His mother asks on the phone whether he has saved anything, and he changes the topic. Hardik, who earns less as a school office clerk, somehow has money left every month. Bhavesh cannot work out how.

ask.q: Bhavesh works hard but is broke by the twentieth of every month. What should he look at first?
o: Ask his manager for a raise, since more salary will fix it
Where his money goes, and what each thing he owns costs him monthly
A personal loan to cover the gap at month end
ask.why: Bhavesh's problem is not effort. A raise often gets swallowed by the same habits, and a loan adds yet another monthly payment. Looking at where his money actually goes shows him which things quietly drain him every month, and that is the first step to changing the pattern.

chapters.take: Earning more does not help if money leaks out as fast as it comes in.

story.b: On Sunday, Bhavesh and Hardik sit on the balcony of their rented flat in Navrangpura with a sheet of paper and two cups of tea. Bhavesh lists everything he owns and marks each item. The phone on EMI takes money out. The upgraded bike takes money out every month through the EMI, petrol and insurance. The gym membership he never uses takes money out. Then Hardik shows his own list. A small fixed deposit pays him interest. An old sewing machine at his family home earns his mother a few thousand rupees a month stitching blouses for neighbours. Bhavesh stares at his page. He always called his bike an asset because it was expensive. It has never put a single rupee in his pocket.

ask.q: A colleague says a big new TV on easy EMI is a smart buy. What should Bhavesh do?
o: Skip it for now, since it takes money out every month and brings nothing in
Buy it, because anything expensive counts as an asset
Buy it, since the EMI is small enough not to notice
ask.why: An asset puts money into your pocket and a liability takes it out. The TV has a big price tag, but it brings nothing in and adds another monthly payment. Small EMIs are exactly how Bhavesh's salary disappeared before. Skipping it keeps his money free for something that pays him.

chapters.take: If it takes money out every month, it is not an asset, however shiny.

story.b: Bhavesh opens his payslip properly for the first time. Gross pay, net pay, EPF, professional tax. He has seen these words for four years and never asked what they meant. That week, colleagues at the chai stall outside a hospital talk about SIPs and credit scores, and he nods along as if he understands. Riding home, he admits to himself that he does not. So he makes a small rule. Every night after dinner, he spends fifteen minutes on one money topic and writes a line about it in a notebook. On the third night he reads how credit card interest works. He checks his own card statement and goes quiet. Paying only the minimum has been costing him far more than he thought.

ask.q: Bhavesh's friends talk about SIPs and index funds, and he just nods along. What is his best move?
o: Copy whatever his friends are investing in
Stay away from money topics, since school never taught him
Learn one money idea in plain words every day, a few minutes at a time
ask.why: Money is a skill anyone can learn, a little at a time. Copying friends means betting on choices he does not understand, and staying away keeps him stuck. Learning one idea a day, like how EPF or card interest works, slowly lets Bhavesh make his own decisions.

chapters.take: Money knowledge is a skill, and fifteen minutes a day is enough to start.

story.b: His regional manager mentions a weekend course in healthcare sales management. It costs thirty thousand rupees, and Bhavesh's first thought is a flat no. That is not for people like him. Then he catches himself. A flat no ends the thinking. So he writes it as a question in his notebook. What would it take to make this possible? The question keeps him awake, in a good way. Next morning he asks HR and learns the company pays half the fee for approved courses, a rule he never read. For the other half, he works out that cooking dinner four nights a week would save about five thousand a month. Three months of dal, rice and the occasional burnt roti would cover it.

ask.q: Hardik wants evening accounting classes but says a laptop is simply too expensive. What should Bhavesh encourage him to do?
o: Drop the classes, since the price is the price
Turn the no into a question and look for options, like a used laptop or the college lab
Buy the newest model on a credit card and sort it out later
ask.why: A flat no shuts Hardik's thinking down, and a credit card adds costly debt, which Bhavesh has just learned about. Asking what would make it possible sends him looking for real options, like a used laptop or the college lab. The point is not spending more, but thinking harder.

chapters.take: A flat no stops your thinking. A good question puts it to work.

story.b: Two offers land in the same week. A pharma distributor offers Bhavesh a desk job with four thousand rupees more a month, mostly entering orders into software. His own company offers him a bigger territory, with hospital purchase teams to negotiate with and two junior reps to guide. The salary there stays the same for now. Hardik says the choice is obvious, take the money. Bhavesh thinks it over with a cutting chai at a stall near Law Garden. He asks himself what each job will make him able to do in five years. The desk job will teach him to type faster. The territory will teach him to sell, negotiate and lead people, skills that would work in any company.

ask.q: Bhavesh must choose between a slightly better paid routine desk job and a role that teaches negotiation and leading people. What should guide him?
o: Only the salary, because money now matters most
Whichever job is less tiring day to day
What each job will teach him, since those skills pay off for years
ask.why: Four thousand rupees more a month is real, but a routine desk job teaches little. Negotiation, selling to hospitals and leading juniors are skills that keep paying for life. Picking the easiest job feels good now but narrows his future. Treating skills as an asset helps Bhavesh choose well.

chapters.take: Pick work for what it teaches, not only for what it pays this month.

story.b: Bhavesh used to save whatever was left on the thirtieth. There was never anything left. Now, on the evening before salary day, he sets up two automatic transfers in his banking app. Five thousand rupees moves into a recurring deposit on the first of every month, and one thousand goes into a small account he calls his learning fund. The money leaves before he even sees the full salary. The first month feels tight. He skips a weekend trip to Mount Abu with friends and cooks more. By the third month he barely notices. His mother asks again whether he has saved anything. This time he sends her a screenshot, and she replies with three smiling faces.

ask.q: Hardik's cousin saves whatever is left at month end, which is usually nothing. What should she change?
o: Move a fixed amount to savings the day salary lands, then live on the rest
Try harder to spend less, then save the balance on the thirtieth
Wait until she earns more before saving anything at all
ask.why: Saving what is left rarely works, because spending always finds a way to use up the month. Waiting for a bigger salary just delays the habit. Moving a fixed amount on salary day protects it before it can be spent, and she learns to live on the rest.

chapters.take: Pay yourself first, on salary day, before the month gets a vote.

story.b: Bhavesh still rides the same bike, now fully paid off, and he has stopped thinking about upgrading it. The phone EMI ended in April, and he did not replace the phone. His recurring deposit grows quietly every month, and his learning fund now buys books on selling and negotiation. The healthcare sales course helped him more than he expected in the new territory, and his manager has started sending him to the toughest hospital meetings. On salary day he still feels a small thrill, but now it lasts the whole month. He reads about one money topic most nights and has filled half a notebook. Hardik jokes that Bhavesh has become the boring friend who asks whether things bring money in or take it out. Bhavesh takes it as praise.

chapters.take: Wealth starts quietly, with what you keep and what you learn, not what you show.
